name: Commodity trend following
heading: The Structural Opportunity: Persistent Supply-Driven Price Trends
caseLead: Commodity price trends can persist because producers cannot quickly adjust output to changes in demand or supply. Supply constraints are particularly important in energy, metals and agriculture, where sanctions, production cuts and weather disruptions can keep markets tight for months.
caseRest: Commodity price trends can reverse quickly when supply returns, demand weakens or producers change output plans. These reversals often follow policy decisions, such as changes in OPEC output targets or in the margin requirements set by exchanges, and they can erase the gains from a long trend. The strategy also lags in range-bound markets, because trend signals reverse repeatedly and each trade incurs costs.
figNote: Each card shows the change in the price of the commodity named in the text, over the period described. Commodity trend following earns from sustained price moves in either direction, so a larger move offers more to follow.

events.title: Oil collapses from record to crisis low
events.text: From July to December 2008, WTI crude fell about 77% as the financial crisis cut demand, after a rise to a record above 145 dollars a barrel. The strategy gained because it held long positions on the way up and then built short positions.

events.title: Margin increases end the silver rally
events.text: In the week to 6 May 2011, silver fell about 27% after the exchange raised margin requirements five times in nine days. The strategy lost because long positions built during the rise were closed at sharply lower prices.

events.title: OPEC keeps output high as oil prices fall
events.text: Between June 2014 and January 2016, Brent crude fell about 76% after OPEC decided in November 2014 not to cut output despite rising US shale supply. The strategy gained because short positions captured a steady decline over several quarters.

events.title: Drone strikes on Saudi oil sites spike prices
events.text: Brent rose about 15% on 16 September 2019 after drone strikes on Saudi Arabian oil facilities halved the country's output, then gave back the gain within two weeks. The strategy lost because the spike reversed before a trend could form.

events.title: Saudi price war meets Covid demand loss
events.text: Brent fell about 24% on 9 March 2020 after Saudi Arabia began a price war with Russia while Covid cut demand. Results were mixed because short oil positions gained, but sharp reversals in metals and grain contracts offset part of the gain.

events.title: Ukraine invasion starts an energy price trend
events.text: Brent rose about 60% from early January to 8 March 2022 as Russia's invasion of Ukraine threatened energy exports. The strategy gained because long positions in oil, gas and wheat rewarded a trend that lasted for several months.

instrument: Futures on energy, metals and agricultural commodities; about 25 contracts; held for weeks; rolled monthly
rules: Long when the 1-month and 6-month price trends both rise, short when both fall; positions reduced when volatility rises; contracts rolled before expiry
costs: Estimated commissions, bid-ask spreads and futures roll costs deducted at each trade
constructionTitle: Strategy construction, from supply-driven trends to diversified risk

legs.instrument: Crude oil, natural gas and heating oil futures
Wheat, corn, soybean and sugar futures
legs.purpose: Earns trends from weather and harvests

legs.position: Long or short soft commodity and livestock futures

size: Set to a 10% annualised volatility target, with each market at most 8% of risk
exit: Position closed when the 1-month trend turns against the 6-month trend
stop: Market position closed after a loss of 1.5% of portfolio value
marketWatch: Rehyn watches inventory levels, the shape of futures curves and the share of supply held by producers that coordinate output, because these show how long a supply-driven trend can last. Rising volatility in oil and metals contracts signals a higher risk of reversal. Production decisions by OPEC and its partners, sanctions announcements and weather in major growing regions are the events most likely to start or end a trend.

favourable.heading: Persistent supply disruptions
favourable.text: Supply disruptions favour the strategy because producers and importers take months to replace lost output, so prices keep moving after the first reaction. After Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Brent rose about 60% in two months and stayed above its starting level through the summer.

favourable.heading: Oversupply from producer decisions
favourable.text: A decision by producers to keep output high favours the strategy because inventories build for many months and prices fall steadily. OPEC's November 2014 decision contributed to a Brent decline of about 76% from June 2014 to January 2016.

favourable.heading: Strong industrial demand cycles
favourable.text: Rapid growth in industrial demand favours the strategy because inventories fall and prices rise over several quarters. After the 2008 financial crisis, Chinese stimulus helped copper more than triple from its December 2008 low to February 2011.

adverse.heading: Policy changes that cap rallies
adverse.text: Exchange and government decisions hurt the strategy when they trigger sharp reversals in trending markets. In May 2011, five margin increases in nine days sent silver down about 27% in a week and forced long positions to close.

adverse.heading: Short spikes without follow-through
adverse.text: Brief spikes hurt the strategy because trend signals confirm after the move, so positions are held as prices return to earlier levels. Drone strikes on Saudi oil facilities lifted Brent about 15% on 16 September 2019, and the gain was reversed within two weeks.

adverse.heading: Rebounds after long declines
adverse.text: Sharp rebounds hurt the strategy because short positions built during a long decline lose when supply cuts or a demand recovery lift prices quickly. In 2016, Brent rose from under 30 dollars in January to above 50 dollars by June, erasing earlier gains from short positions.

infoHist: Historical results show the strategy's peak-to-trough drawdown during each event, measured from its value just before the event to its lowest point using the default backtest parameters above. Each event window runs from the last market high before the shock to the market low.
infoForward: Scenario results show the estimated profit or loss over the first month of each scenario. Rehyn's scenario engine projects moves in oil, metals and agricultural prices, which are then applied to the strategy's current positions.
